name: Midnight Green
lede: Midnight Green is a near-black teal, a landscape-and-time-of-day compound that our library files as the darkest member of the midnight family of names.

sections.title: A midnight shade
sections.body:
The nearest named colors on file are [[deep-teal]], [[dark-teal]] and [[dark-delft-blue]], at 5, 5 and 6.2 ΔE [2]. The hex #004953 measures a dark greenish blue in ISCC-NBS terms, 4.8 units from the nearest named block, and sits near 1.0B 2.7/4.1 in Munsell notation [2]. Who first paired "midnight" with "green" is not recorded in the sources we checked, so the coinage itself stays undocumented [1]. The closest listed library neighbor is [[petrol]], a similarly dark blue-green, 7.2 units away [2]. A nearer sibling in name is [[teal]], the hue family it sits within once the "midnight" modifier is stripped away [1].

On screen the color reads almost as a dark teal rather than true black. Its lightness value, 28 out of 100, puts it well above black [2]. It still reads as "midnight" because green light drops out fastest in low light, leaving blue to dominate what little color the eye can still register.

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: Our archive finds a close match to Midnight Green in 61 of 23,781 paintings, 0.26 percent, with the within-painting test narrowing that to 28 [3]. That makes it rarer than roughly 58 percent of the named colors we track [3]. It peaks in the 1400s, in 6 of 945 paintings, present in 0.6 percent of our paintings from that century against a baseline that makes it 2.7 times more likely than chance, and the earliest match is a 1310 panel attributed to Giotto, a floor and not a first, since the archive's early centuries are thin [3]. Inside the paintings that carry it, the color plays a hidden color more than half the time, the kind of dark passage a painting's lightness order places near the bottom without the viewer necessarily noticing it as a distinct hue [3]. All of this describes photographs of aged, varnished panels, not a pigment identification [3].
